newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia still must reform despite growth - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia still must reform despite growth - analysts.

text.p: A predicted slowdown in the rapid growth of Slovakia's economy appears to reflect a lack of industrial reforms, analysts said after digesting first half gross domestic product (GDP) results.

Stefan Condik, chairman of the Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) in presenting the lastest GDP figures for this year on Wednesday, revised his previous forecast for 1996 GDP growth to 6.4 to 7.0 percent from a previous 7.1 percent.
Although the growth figure remains robust, Condik said industrial reforms had generally run into a wall.
"The urgently-needed industry restructuring is stagnating," Condik told reporters. "What is being restructured in the country is simply households."
SUSR said Slovakia's GDP growth slowed to 6.9 percent in the second quarter from 7.3 percent in the first quarter, and the growth was mainly due to higher household consumption.
Condik warned that his forecast could even turn out to be too optimistic if the country's central bank adopted further restrictive policy measures to stem domestic consumption.
Domestic demand has dominated Slovakia's economic growth as exports, the main growth motor in the past, have stagnated.
Exports accounted for only 55.6 percent of GDP in the first half compared with 66 percent in the same period last year, partly as a result year of the economic slowdown in the West.
The country's central bank and macroeconomic analysts, whose GDP forecasts have always been more conservative, have suggested the new growth engine may not be so reliable.
"The figures obscure the need for higher foreign investment and restructuring," Martin Barto, an anlyst with ING Barings Bratislava, told Reuters.
Industrial output in June, according to the latests figures, contracted for the second time in three months, with year-on-year output falling 1.8 percent in that month.

"Restructuring has not happened, and thus a drop in exports will eventually result in a decline in domestic demand, probably around the end of the year," added Juraj Rencko, an analyst with the Slovak Academy of Science.
The switch to demand-driven GDP joined a surge in short-term lending, which led the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) to implement a series of measures in July aimed at tightening the money supply.
The moves included hikes in the Lombard last-resort lending facility and minimum reserve requirements for banks, which boosted the interbank money market rates to a 13-14 percent.
But Condik said the economy had not yet overheated.
"We still could have waited (on raising interest rates), the inflation developments favoured that," he said.
Slovakia's key money supply measure, M2, rose 21.0 percent year-on-year in July, compared to a full-year target of an expansion of 11.6 percent year-on-year.
Still lowest in eastern Europe, Slovak inflation rose to 5.6 percent year-on-year in August, from 5.5 percent in July.
"There are no short-term solutions to the growth slowdown," Rencko said. "Rather than in inflation, I see a greater risk (of the domestic demand-driven GDP) in a current account deficit."
The Slovak current account deficit hit $737.1 million in the first half of 1996, compared with a surplus of $412.3 million in the first half of 1995.
